artiest/the-crickets.text:
The Crickets were an American rock 'n' roll band from Lubbock, Texas, formed in January 1957 by singer and songwriter Buddy Holly. The original line-up consisted of Holly on vocals and lead guitar, Niki Sullivan on rhythm guitar, Jerry Allison on drums and Joe B. Mauldin on bass. Holly had been recording demos with friends since 1954 and had made an unsuccessful album for Decca in 1956. Real success came when producer Norman Petty recorded his music in Clovis, New Mexico. Because Holly had already recorded under his own name, he needed a new group name. The band members first looked at names of birds and then moved on to insects. They very nearly settled on Beetles.

That'll Be the Day was released in May 1957 and reached number one on the American Top 100 in September. The debut album was called The Chirping Crickets. Petty had the recordings released under two names, Buddy Holly and the Crickets, so that DJs would play the records more often. In August 1957 they were the first white act to appear at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and in 1958 they played fifty concerts in twenty-five days in the United Kingdom. Holly then went on alone and was killed in a plane crash in 1959. The Crickets continued to perform and record in changing line-ups, into the twenty-first century.

What matters most for pop history is their set-up: guitar, bass and drums, playing their own songs. It became the model for later rock bands. The Beatles took their name partly as a tribute to the Crickets, and added a pun of their own: beetles for the insects, and beat for the rhythm.
artiest/the-crickets.listen: Listen to That'll Be the Day by The Crickets. Notice the simple line-up of guitar, bass and drums, and Buddy Holly's slightly hiccupping singing style.

artiest/the-cure.text:
The Cure are an English band from Crawley, south of London. The group began in 1976 as Malice, were called Easy Cure in 1977 and have been The Cure since 1978. Singer and guitarist Robert Smith is the only member who has always been part of the band. The Cure grew out of post-punk and became one of the bands that shaped gothic rock.

The first records, with the single Killing an Arab (1978) and the album Three Imaginary Boys (1979), were dry, fast guitar pop. With Seventeen Seconds (1980), produced by Smith and Mike Hedges, the sound became darker and emptier. A Forest, the first single from that album, released in April 1980, became the band's first hit, reaching number 31 in the UK. Guitar and bass repeat short motifs in a sea of reverb, and Hedges used several flangers to make the guitar float. Faith (1981) and above all Pornography (1982) made the sound heavier still. Smith's black clothes, tousled hair and lipstick became the uniform of the goths.

In the 1980s The Cure alternated dark albums with pop singles. Disintegration (1989) reached number 3 in the UK, and Lovesong, which reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100, became their only American top ten hit. The band has sold more than thirty million records and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2019. In 2024 Songs of a Lost World was released, the first album of new work in sixteen years, and it reached number 1 in the UK.
artiest/the-cure.listen: In A Forest, listen to Robert Smith's guitar: through flanger effects the sound ripples and floats, as if you were looking through mist. Notice also the bass of Simon Gallup, which keeps playing the same short motif, and the ending of the album version, in which the instruments drop out one by one.

artiest/the-damned.text:
The Damned are an English rock band from London, formed in 1976 by singer Dave Vanian, guitarist Brian James, bassist Captain Sensible and drummer Rat Scabies. Vanian, Sensible and Scabies had previously played together in Masters of the Backside, a band that also included Chrissie Hynde. They played their first gig on 6 July 1976, supporting the Sex Pistols at the 100 Club in London.

On 22 October 1976 New Rose was released on Stiff Records, the first punk single from the United Kingdom. That was five weeks before Anarchy in the U.K. by the Sex Pistols. The B-side was a fast version of Help! by the Beatles. In December 1976 they joined the Anarchy Tour, until Malcolm McLaren threw them off the tour. The album Damned Damned Damned, produced by Nick Lowe, was released in February 1977 and was the first album by a British punk band. The first American tour by a British punk group was theirs as well. After the unsuccessful Music for Pleasure in 1977 the band briefly split up. Without James they returned with Machine Gun Etiquette in 1979.

In the 1980s they chose a gothic and psychedelic sound, with The Black Album in 1980, Strawberries in 1982, Phantasmagoria in 1985 and Anything in 1986. Nine singles reached the British top 40 in that period. Later came Not of This Earth in 1995, Grave Disorder in 2001, So, Who's Paranoid? in 2008, Evil Spirits in 2018 and Darkadelic in 2023. The Damned are regarded as influential for punk rock, gothic rock and hardcore punk. They showed that punk could be more than anger alone: it could also be humour, theatre and melody.
artiest/the-damned.listen: Listen to New Rose by The Damned. Notice the furious tempo, the raw guitars and the way the vocals drive the song forward in just a few minutes.

artiest/the-dap-kings.text:
Sharon Jones & the Dap-Kings were an American funk and soul band on Daptone Records, part of a revival of the funk and soul of the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. Its roots lie with the Soul Providers of Gabriel Roth, also known as Bosco Mann, and Phillip Lehman, who started the label Desco Records in the 1990s. Sharon Jones, then still a prison guard, sang backing vocals and was discovered that way.

When Roth and Lehman parted ways in 2000, Roth started Daptone Records with saxophonist Neal Sugarman. A new group emerged, the Dap-Kings, with among others Roth on bass, Sugarman on saxophone, guitarist Binky Griptite, tenor saxophonist Leon Michels and drummer Homer Steinweiss. The debut album Dap-Dippin' with Sharon Jones and the Dap-Kings came out in 2002, followed by Naturally (2005) and 100 Days, 100 Nights (2007). The 2014 album Give the People What They Want was nominated for a Grammy.

The Dap-Kings are also known as Daptone's house band, above all for their collaboration with Mark Ronson, including on Back to Black by Amy Winehouse. The sound is that of analogue recordings with a tight, rhythmic horn section, in the tradition of James Brown. After the death of Sharon Jones in 2016, the album Soul of a Woman was released in 2017. The band kept playing together until 2018. Their work showed that old soul and funk can still sound alive.
artiest/the-dap-kings.listen: Listen to Back to Black by Amy Winehouse and notice the horns and the rhythm underneath, played by the Dap-Kings. Can you hear how the recording sounds like a record from the 1960s?

artiest/the-dave-clark-five.text:
The Dave Clark Five, also known as the DC5, were an English rock 'n' roll band from Tottenham in London. The group began in 1958 as the backing band of singer Stan Saxon and carried on as an independent group in 1962. The regular line-up consisted of drummer Dave Clark, bassist Rick Huxley, lead guitarist Lenny Davidson, saxophonist Denis Payton and keyboardist and singer Mike Smith. Clark was leader, producer, manager and co-writer, and made sure he kept hold of the master tapes.

The group was promoted as the Tottenham Sound, an answer to the Mersey Beat from Liverpool. That sound was loud and driving, with Clark's hard drumming, Payton's saxophone and Smith's rough voice. In January 1964 Glad All Over reached the top of the British chart, knocking I Want to Hold Your Hand by the Beatles off the top spot. Other hits were Bits and Pieces, Can't You See That She's Mine, Catch Us If You Can and Everybody Knows. In the United States their version of Over and Over by Bobby Day reached number one in December 1965. After the Beatles they were the second group of the British Invasion to appear on The Ed Sullivan Show, on which they performed eighteen times. In 1965 they starred in the film Catch Us If You Can, directed by John Boorman.

With the exception of a few songs, the group did not follow the psychedelic trend. In the United States their popularity faded around 1967, and in 1970 they split up. In 2008 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. They were among the commercially most successful bands of the British Invasion, and showed that English beat music did not have to come from Liverpool alone.
artiest/the-dave-clark-five.listen: Listen to Glad All Over by The Dave Clark Five. Notice the heavy, stomping drums of Dave Clark and the rough singing of Mike Smith.

artiest/the-del-tones.text:
The Del-Tones is the original name of the Canadian rock group The Beau-Marks, formed in Montreal, Quebec, in 1958. Under that first name the single Rockin' Blues was released in April 1959, with Moonlight Party on the B-side. Shortly afterwards the group changed its name, as a nod to the Bomarc, a missile. Its members included guitarist Ray Hutchinson, guitarist and bassist Mike Robitaille, pianist and singer Joey Fréchette and drummer Gilles Tailleur.

Their breakthrough was Clap Your Hands. The song topped the charts in Canada and Australia, reached number 45 on the American Billboard chart and also did well in New Zealand. French-language versions were released too, among them under the title Frappe Tes Mains. In 1960 the first album came out, The High Flying Beau-Marks, with ten songs. The band appeared on American Bandstand and at a charity concert at Carnegie Hall.

The Beau-Marks were the first Canadian band to headline at the Peppermint Lounge in New York and to be invited onto The Ed Sullivan Show. Two more albums followed, after which the group disbanded in 1963. At a reunion in 1968 Clap Your Hands was reissued. It was a simple rock 'n' roll sound with guitars, piano and a solid rhythm, typical of the pop music of the late 1950s.
artiest/the-del-tones.listen: Listen to Clap Your Hands and notice the simple structure of the song. Can you hear how such a simple idea can carry a dance record?

artiest/the-del-vikings.text:
The Del-Vikings, also spelled The Dell-Vikings, were an American doo-wop group. They formed in 1955 among servicemen of the United States Air Force in Pittsburgh, with among others Clarence Quick and Kripp Johnson. Because the members were in the service, the group constantly ran the risk of someone being transferred. Remarkably, it was a mixed group, with black and white singers, at a time when that was rare.

Their first hit came in 1957 with Come Go with Me, written by Clarence Quick. The song reached number five on the American pop chart. Later that year came Whispering Bells, with Kripp Johnson as lead singer. Come Go with Me was later used in films such as American Graffiti and Stand by Me. That made it a soundtrack of the 1950s, even for people who did not know the record from that time.

In 1957 the group became stuck in a contract dispute. Most of the members were minors when they signed and were able to free themselves from the small label Fee Bee. They went to Mercury, while Johnson remained tied to Fee Bee and Dot. For a while there were therefore two Del-Vikings. The group broke up and was later reassembled. In 1960 they signed with ABC Records, but new hits failed to appear and in 1965 the group disbanded. A reunion followed in 1970, and in 1973 a new version of Come Go with Me was recorded.
artiest/the-del-vikings.listen: Listen to Come Go with Me and notice how the group harmony carries the melody. Can you hear how the lead singer and the other voices complement one another?

artiest/the-dollar-brand-trio.text:
The Dollar Brand Trio was the name under which the South African pianist Dollar Brand performed in Europe in the early 1960s. He was born in Cape Town in 1934 as Adolph Johannes Brand and grew up in the city's harbour districts, where he heard marabi, mbaqanga, church music and American jazz. Later, as a Muslim, he took the name Abdullah Ibrahim.

In 1962 he moved to Europe. His future wife, the singer Sathima Bea Benjamin, persuaded Duke Ellington, who was on tour in Zurich, to come and listen to the trio at the Africana Club in February 1963. Ellington was impressed and helped arrange a recording session with Reprise Records. The result was the record Duke Ellington presents The Dollar Brand Trio. It was an important step in an international career: Brand went on to play at many European festivals, and in 1965 he moved to New York.

His piano playing shows the influence of Thelonious Monk and Duke Ellington, mixed with African and Cape music. In 1974 he recorded Mannenberg in Cape Town, a piece that became an anthem against apartheid. Ibrahim is regarded as the most important figure of Cape jazz. The Zurich trio belongs at the start of that story, when a musician from South Africa brought his own sound into the jazz world.
artiest/the-dollar-brand-trio.listen: Listen to Mannenberg by Abdullah Ibrahim, as Dollar Brand was later called, which was recorded in one take during a collective improvisation. Can you hear how the musicians listen to one another?

artiest/the-dominoes.text:
Billy Ward and his Dominoes were an American R&B group and one of the most successful vocal groups of the early 1950s. The leader, Billy Ward, was a pianist, arranger and vocal coach. He had studied in Chicago and at the Juilliard School in New York, something unusual for a black musician at the time. Together with his business partner Rose Marks he put together a group from his pupils, with Clyde McPhatter as lead tenor, whom he had heard after a win on Amateur Night at the Apollo Theater.

The group signed with Federal Records and called itself the Dominoes. In 1951 it had its first R&B hit with Do Something For Me. Then came Sixty Minute Man, with bass singer Bill Brown as lead vocalist. The song spent fourteen weeks at the top of the R&B chart and also reached the pop chart. The lyrics went further than was usual at the time, and the song appealed to black and white audiences alike. It is considered a candidate for the first rock 'n' roll record. In 1952 came Have Mercy Baby.

Ward was a strict leader who fined his singers and paid them little. In 1953 McPhatter left to start the Drifters. Later Jackie Wilson also became a member of the group. In this way the Dominoes helped launch two great singers. Their blend of gospel singing and blues, on the border between R&B and rock and roll, became an example for later groups.
artiest/the-dominoes.listen: Listen to Sixty Minute Man and notice the voice of bass singer Bill Brown as lead vocalist. Can you hear why this song is one of the candidates for the first rock 'n' roll record?

artiest/the-doors.text:
The Doors were an American rock band, formed in Los Angeles in 1965 by singer Jim Morrison, keyboardist Ray Manzarek, guitarist Robby Krieger and drummer John Densmore. The name comes from The Doors of Perception, a book by Aldous Huxley, which in turn quotes a line by William Blake. With long, dark songs and the poetry of Morrison they became an important band of American psychedelic rock.

In 1966 they were the house band at the Whisky a Go Go in Los Angeles and signed with Elektra. The debut album The Doors was released in January 1967. Light My Fire became Elektra's first single to reach number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album closes with The End, almost twelve minutes long. The band had no bassist of its own: live, Manzarek played the bass lines with his left hand on a keyboard bass, alongside his organ. In the studio, session bassists were mostly hired from the second album onwards. Morrison pushed the limits. After a chaotic concert in Miami in 1969 he was convicted of indecent exposure; in 2010 he received a posthumous pardon.

The last album with Morrison, L.A. Woman, was released in 1971 and closes with Riders on the Storm. In July 1971 Morrison was found dead in Paris, aged 27. He is buried at Père Lachaise. The band has sold more than a hundred million records worldwide and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1993. Post-punk singers such as Ian Curtis of Joy Division and Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen were later often compared to Morrison.
artiest/the-doors.listen: In Riders on the Storm, listen to the electric piano sound of Ray Manzarek: a soft, rippling Fender Rhodes, with the bass of Jerry Scheff beneath it. The rain and thunder come from a sound-effects record, and Morrison whispers his lyrics once more over the vocal, like an echo.

artiest/the-dorsey-brothers.text:
The Dorsey Brothers were an American studio dance band led by the brothers Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey. They began recording for OKeh Records in 1928 and made recordings for all kinds of small labels. In 1934 they signed with Decca and formed a touring orchestra, with Tommy as frontman, in an unusual line-up of one trumpet, three trombones, three saxophones and four rhythm players. Glenn Miller wrote a few numbers for the orchestra in that period, among them Annie's Cousin Fannie and Dese Dem Dose.

The brothers clashed constantly. In May 1935 Tommy walked out during a performance after a quarrel about the tempo of a song. In that same year the orchestra had two number ones on Decca, including Lullaby of Broadway with Bob Crosby as vocalist. Tommy then started his own orchestra and Jimmy continued the old one.

Yet the brothers later came together again. In 1945 they recorded a V-Disc, in 1947 they appeared in the film The Fabulous Dorseys, and from 1950 Jimmy was part of Tommy's orchestra. In 1954 they got their own television series, Stage Show, from Jackie Gleason. In it Elvis Presley made his national television debut in 1956. Tommy died in November 1956, Jimmy in June 1957. In 1996 the United States Postal Service issued a stamp in honour of both. The Dorsey Brothers show how the big-band era sounded before rock and roll changed popular music.
artiest/the-dorsey-brothers.listen: Listen to Lullaby of Broadway from 1935 and notice Bob Crosby's singing among the horns. Can you hear how a dance orchestra of that era forms one whole together with a singer?

artiest/the-dream.text:
The-Dream is the stage name of Terius Nash, born in 1977 in Rockingham, North Carolina, and raised in Atlanta. He is a singer, songwriter and producer in R&B and hip hop. After the death of his mother, when he was fifteen, he began writing songs. He played trumpet, drums and guitar. In 2001 he came into contact with producer Laney Stewart and was given a publishing deal after writing Everything for B2K. Together with Laney's brother Christopher Tricky Stewart he later wrote Umbrella for Rihanna (2007) and Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) for Beyoncé (2008). Among other things he also co-wrote Me Against the Music for Britney Spears and Baby for Justin Bieber.

As an artist he signed with Def Jam. His debut album Love/Hate was released in 2007 and was written and recorded in eight days. Love vs. Money (2009), Love King (2010), 1977 (2011) and IV Play (2013) followed. His sound is smooth, modern R&B, with songs about love and relationships. Later, through his own label Radio Killa Records, he released among other things the triple release Ménage à Trois: Sextape Vol. 1, 2, 3.

His greatest influence lies behind the scenes. He wrote for many pop stars and won eight Grammys. Single Ladies won the Grammy for Song of the Year and Best R&B Song. In this way The-Dream belongs among the writers who shaped the sound of pop in the 2000s, often without the public knowing his name.
artiest/the-dream.listen: Listen to Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) by Beyoncé, which The-Dream wrote. Notice the tight rhythm and the chorus that sticks immediately. What makes this chorus so easy to sing along to?

artiest/the-drifters.text:
The Drifters are an American pop and R&B/soul group. The first group formed in 1953 around Clyde McPhatter, the lead tenor of Billy Ward and his Dominoes. Ahmet Ertegun of Atlantic Records sought him out and had him put together a group of his own. McPhatter wanted to mix gospel and secular music and recruited singers from his church choir, but after a first session that line-up proved not to work. A second line-up made Money Honey, their first big hit in 1953.

The group is remarkable because there was hardly ever a fixed line-up. George Treadwell had owned the name since 1955 and kept hiring new singers, at low pay. Over the years the Treadwell group counted sixty musicians. A second group, which formed around Ben E. King in 1959, received its own place in the Vocal Group Hall of Fame. There are three golden periods: the early 1950s, the 1960s and the early 1970s.

The Drifters had six number ones on the R&B chart: Money Honey (1953), Honey Love (1954), Adorable (1955), There Goes My Baby (1959), Save the Last Dance for Me (1960) and Under the Boardwalk (1964). Their greatest successes in England came in the 1970s, with Kissin' in the Back Row of the Movies. The sound links gospel singing with pop and soul. Many later vocal groups learned from the way the Drifters brought singing and arrangement together.
artiest/the-drifters.listen: Listen to Save the Last Dance for Me and notice how the vocals and the rhythm of the song together create a danceable atmosphere. What tells you that this is soul and not rock and roll?

artiest/the-early-music-consort-of-londo.text:
The Early Music Consort of London was a British ensemble of the late 1960s and the 1970s that specialised in historically informed performances of medieval and Renaissance music. The group was founded in 1967 by the musicologists David Munrow and Christopher Hogwood, who had studied together at Pembroke College, Cambridge. Munrow took inspiration from the Alte Musik movement in Germany and wanted to arouse interest in early music in England too.

The group was small and versatile, designed for touring but able to be expanded for recordings. In the original line-up Munrow played many different wind instruments, and Hogwood keyboard, harp and percussion. Others included Mary Remnant on fiddle, Oliver Brookes on viola da gamba, Robert Spencer on lute and countertenor James Bowman. The group made influential recordings, such as The Six Wives of Henry VIII (1970), Music of the Crusades (1971), The Art of Courtly Love (1973) and The Art of the Netherlands (1976).

A recording from 1976, The Fairie Round by Anthony Holborne, was chosen by NASA for the Voyager Golden Record, which went into space in 1977 with the Voyager 1 and 2 space probes. Munrow played the bass sordune on it. The group ceased in 1976 after the death of Munrow. Its name is regarded as one of the drivers of the British early-music revival in the late twentieth century.
artiest/the-early-music-consort-of-londo.listen: Listen to The Fairie Round by Anthony Holborne in this ensemble's performance and notice the different wind instruments. This piece travels on the Voyager Golden Record: why might it have been chosen as an example of Western music?

artiest/the-east-side-boyz.text:
Lil Jon & the East Side Boyz were a hip hop group from Atlanta. Jonathan Smith, who became known as Lil Jon, formed the group in 1995 with Big Sam and Lil' Bo. Smith was first a club DJ and worked for Jermaine Dupri's label So So Def. His group called its music crunk: an energetic, club-oriented style of hip hop. Their first single Who U Wit? from 1996 is seen as the song that brought the word crunk into hip hop. In 1997 the first album was released, Get Crunk, Who U Wit: Da Album, and in 2000 the breakthrough album We Still Crunk!!.

Bryan Leach, an A&R man who saw the group perform in Atlanta, compared the energy to that of the young Beastie Boys, a rock group that rapped. In 2002 the group signed with TVT Records. The second studio album brought Get Low, with Ying Yang Twins, which was a success in the nightclubs and reached the top ten of the Billboard Hot 100. The last studio album, Crunk Juice (2004), contained Lovers and Friends with Usher and Ludacris, which reached number three on the Hot 100. In 2005 the group split up.

In the 2000s Lil Jon also produced for others, including Yeah! by Usher and Goodies by Ciara. In this way he defined the sound of crunk and brought the style out of the clubs of Atlanta and into the charts.
artiest/the-east-side-boyz.listen: Listen to Get Low and notice the rhythm and the repetition in the vocals. Can you hear why a song like this works instantly in a club?

artiest/the-edge.text:
The Edge is the stage name of David Howell Evans, born on 8 August 1961 in England to Welsh parents and raised in Dublin. He is lead guitarist, keyboardist and backing vocalist of the rock band U2. In 1976 he got together with his brother Dik and classmates from Mount Temple Comprehensive School when drummer Larry Mullen Jr. was looking for musicians. Bono and Adam Clayton responded too. In 1978 the band was named U2. He got the nickname the Edge from members of Lypton Village, the circle around Bono.

His guitar playing is unobtrusive but recognisable and defines the sound of U2. It is characterised by clear-sounding tones, rhythmic delay, sustained notes, harmonics and a lot of effects equipment. He often uses a delay set to a dotted eighth note, which makes it seem as though two guitarists are playing. With U2 he made, among others, The Joshua Tree (1987) and Achtung Baby (1991). He also produced, including Zooropa (1993).

Outside the band he worked with Bono on music theatre and on songs for others, such as GoldenEye for Tina Turner. In 1986 he made the film score Captive with Michael Brook, his only solo record. He also wrote music for the musical Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark. He campaigned for human rights and co-founded Music Rising, a charity for musicians affected by Hurricane Katrina. Music magazines count him among the greatest guitarists of all time.
artiest/the-edge.listen: Listen to a U2 song from The Joshua Tree and notice the Edge's guitar: the clear tone and the echo effect that plays along rhythmically. Try to hear where the echo seems to fill in notes that he does not play.

artiest/the-electrifying-mojo.text:
The Electrifying Mojo, born Charles Johnson in Little Rock, Arkansas, is an American radio personality and DJ in Detroit. He began his career at local stations in Little Rock, worked at the University of Michigan's radio station after his service in the air force and ended up at the Detroit station WGPR in 1977. Later he was at WJLB and WHYT, in Toledo and at WMXD, and returned to WGPR in the 1990s. Sometimes he also wrote music, under the name C. J. Surge.

His programme ran from 1977 until the mid-1980s and was broadcast on stations aimed at a black audience. Even so, Mojo played a mix of soul, funk, new wave, hip hop and rock. He introduced artists such as Prince, Parliament-Funkadelic, The B-52's and Kraftwerk to the Detroit audience. On JLB he announced the landing of the mothership every evening at ten o'clock. He liked to play records right to the end, without interfering, and sometimes played the music of Prince for hours, including album tracks and B-sides. He also made themed programmes, for example about symphonic music by black composers or about Duke Ellington.

His influence is found above all in Detroit techno. Juan Atkins, Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May, the three men regarded as the founders of that music, named Mojo as an influence on their development, as did Richie Hawtin, Jeff Mills and Carl Craig. What they heard in him was a radio without genre boundaries: European electronics next to American funk. That gave young musicians in an industrial city an open view of what a machine and a groove could achieve together.
artiest/the-electrifying-mojo.listen: Listen to Trans Europe Express by Kraftwerk, the kind of record Mojo liked to play. Notice the steady, mechanical rhythm, and remember that on his show it sounded right next to funk.

artiest/the-english-concert.text:
The English Concert is a Baroque orchestra from London that plays on historical instruments. It was founded in November 1972 by Trevor Pinnock and others. It began with seven musicians and then grew into the orchestral repertoire. It was one of the first orchestras to focus entirely on Baroque and Classical music on historical instruments, with a repertoire running roughly from Monteverdi to Mozart. Pinnock led the group from the harpsichord for thirty years.

After a debut at the English Bach Festival in 1973, the first record followed in 1974, Sons of Bach, with harpsichord concertos. From 1978 to 1995 the orchestra made many recordings for Archiv Produktion, capturing most of the major Baroque repertoire, among them Water Music, the Brandenburg Concertos and Le quattro stagioni. A choir was also founded in 1983. From 1996 to 2001 the group carried out a large project under the title Great Religious Works of the 18th Century, including Bach's Mass in B Minor, the St. John Passion and the St. Matthew Passion.

In 2003 Pinnock handed over the leadership to the violinist Andrew Manze, who reconstructed the first performance of Handel's Water Music of 1717, sailing along the Thames. In 2007 the harpsichordist Harry Bicket followed. The orchestra belongs to the movements that wanted to make early music sound again as the composers intended, with instruments of their own time.
artiest/the-english-concert.listen: Listen to Water Music by Handel in the performance by The English Concert and notice the sound of the Baroque instruments. Can you hear the differences from a modern symphony orchestra?

artiest/the-everly-brothers.text:
The Everly Brothers were an American duo, consisting of the brothers Don and Phil Everly. They were known for their playing on steel-string acoustic guitars and for their singing in close harmony. They combined rock and roll, country and pop and are regarded as pioneers of country rock. As children they sang on the radio in Iowa in the 1940s with their parents, and later they were spotted in Nashville by Chet Atkins.

Their first big hit was Bye Bye Love, number one in the spring of 1957. In 1958 came Wake Up Little Susie, All I Have to Do Is Dream and Problems. In 1960 they signed with Warner Bros. and made Cathy's Clown, their best-selling single. In 1961 the brothers joined the Marine Corps Reserve, and afterwards their success in the United States declined. In England and Canada they continued to have hits. In 1973 they split up, and in 1983 they reunited.

The duo's influence was great. The harmony singing and the acoustic guitars echoed in The Beatles, The Beach Boys, the Bee Gees and Simon & Garfunkel. In 2015 Rolling Stone ranked them number one on its list of the twenty greatest duos of all time. In 1986 they were included in the first class of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Don Everly received an award for the guitar intro of Wake Up Little Susie. Phil died in 2014, Don in 2021.
artiest/the-everly-brothers.listen: Listen to All I Have to Do Is Dream and notice how the two voices keep singing very close together. Can you hear how the acoustic guitar carries the song?

artiest/the-ex.text:
The Ex is a Dutch underground band that formed in 1979, at the height of the first punk wave, out of the squatters' movement in Amsterdam and Wormer. The first line-up consisted of singer G.W. Sok, guitarist Terrie Hessels, drummer Geurt and bassist René. The band chose its name because it was the shortest on the list and therefore quick to spray on a wall. In 1980 the first EP was released, All Corpses Smell the Same, followed by the debut album Disturbing Domestic Peace. Their lyrics dealt with politics, squatting and social injustice.

Over the decades the band's music became more and more layered. Noise, folk, world music from among others Hungary, Turkey, Ethiopia, Congo and Eritrea, and free jazz were added. The Ex collaborated with, among others, the cellist Tom Cora on Scrabbling at the Lock (1991), with producer Steve Albini on Starters Alternators (1998) and Dizzy Spells (2001), and with Tortoise, Sonic Youth and the Instant Composers Pool Orchestra. The album Instant was an improvised double album. Katherina Bornefeld has played drums since 1984. In 2009 Sok left and was succeeded by Arnold de Boer.

The Ex gave concerts in Ethiopia and brought African bands such as Konono Nr. 1 to Europe and the United States. With more than twenty albums the group is regarded as one of the most important and most independent bands in the Netherlands, internationally praised for its social message and its rhythmic, atonal guitar playing.
artiest/the-ex.listen: Listen to State of Shock from Scrabbling at the Lock and notice the rhythmic guitar playing and the raw vocals. Can you hear how the band mixes punk and experiment?

artiest/the-five-satins.text:
The Five Satins are an American doo-wop group from New Haven, Connecticut. They were formed in 1954 and kept performing until 1994. The group began with six members and later became a quintet. The leader was Fred Parris. In the early years they had little success, until the group reshuffled and recorded the song In the Still of the Night. It was first released on the small local label Standord, and then on the New York label Ember.

In the Still of the Night became a big hit in the United States, and later the song sold more than a million copies. It was originally the B-side of the single The Jones Girl. The song gained a second life when it appeared in 1959 as the opening track on Oldies But Goodies Vol. 1 from Original Sound Records, a series that grew to fifteen volumes. Shortly after the success Parris went into the army, so that the group had to reorganise again. The debut album Presenting The 5 Satins was released in 1957. The group is in the Vocal Group Hall of Fame.

The music of the Five Satins is doo-wop in its muted form: soft harmony singing, a slow, swaying rhythm and a lead who is given space. The song stayed on the radio for decades, and the compilation albums kept it alive.
artiest/the-five-satins.listen: Listen to In the Still of the Nite and notice the backing vocals, which hardly sing any words. Can you hear how they carry the rhythm while the lead singer sings his soft melody?

artiest/the-four-tops.text:
The Four Tops are an American vocal group from Detroit, formed in 1953 as the Four Aims. Singer Levi Stubbs and Abdul Duke Fakir, both from Pershing High, sang at a birthday party with Renaldo Obie Benson and Lawrence Payton of Northern High. They decided to stay together. In 1956 they signed with Chess Records and changed their name to Four Tops, to avoid confusion with the Ames Brothers. For seven years they had no success on all kinds of labels, but they performed a lot and in this way learned a polished stage act. In 1963 Berry Gordy brought them to Motown.

There they became the leading male vocal group of the songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland. It started in 1964 with Baby I Need Your Loving. In 1965 came I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie Honey Bunch), their first number one in the United States, and in 1966 Reach Out I'll Be There, also number one. They also had hits such as It's the Same Old Song, Something About You and Shake Me, Wake Me (When It's Over). In 1973 they achieved another million-seller with Ain't No Woman. The four sang together for more than forty years, until 1997 without a single change in the line-up. In 1990 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

What stood out was Stubbs, a baritone who was made by the writers to sing the highest reaches of his range. That gave his gospel-tinged voice a tense, urgent sound. Together with the Supremes, the Temptations and the Miracles, the Four Tops shaped the Motown sound: polished soul with clear production. For anyone who wants to understand the role of songwriting teams in pop, their work is a fine example: the singers made the songs, but the writers built the sound.
artiest/the-four-tops.listen: Listen to Reach Out I'll Be There by The Four Tops. Notice the high, urgent voice of Levi Stubbs and the driving rhythm that sustains the tension throughout the song.

artiest/the-fugees.text:
The Fugees were an American hip hop group from South Orange, New Jersey. The trio consisted of Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Pras Michel. Hill and Pras met at Columbia High School in Maplewood, and then Wyclef joined them. They began in 1990 as Tranzlator Crew. In 1993 they signed with Ruffhouse Records, a label distributed through Columbia. The new name came from refugee, a word often used disparagingly for Haitian Americans. Jean and Michel themselves have Haitian roots.

Their debut album Blunted on Reality was released on 1 February 1994, after a dispute with the record company, with singles such as Nappy Heads and Vocab. It barely caught on. That did happen with The Score from 1996, with Fu-Gee-La, Killing Me Softly and Ready or Not. The album reached the top of the American album chart and for a time was the best-selling hip hop album ever. It was the second rap album to be nominated for a Grammy for Album of the Year. They also worked with Simply Red on Angel and with Busta Rhymes, A Tribe Called Quest and John Forté on Rumble in the Jungle. They also founded the collective Refugee Camp All-Stars and gave the biggest concert in Haitian history. After that the three went solo. Jean released The Carnival in 1997, with contributions from all three.

The Fugees stood out at a time when gangsta rap dominated. They combined hip hop and R&B with reggae, soul and other music of the Black diaspora, played real instruments and wrote socially conscious lyrics. Lauryn Hill, a singer and rapper at once, went on to have a solo career of her own. They showed that hip hop could also be melodic, warm and broad.
artiest/the-fugees.listen: Listen to Killing Me Softly by the Fugees. Notice how Lauryn Hill's singing lies soft and clear over a calm beat, and how the rap then brings a completely different colour.

artiest/the-funk-brothers.text:
The Funk Brothers were Motown's regular studio musicians in Detroit. From 1959 to 1972 they played the accompaniment on most of the label's recordings. There is no fixed list of members, but the core included pianist and organist Earl Van Dyke, bandleader Joe Hunter, bassist James Jamerson, the drummers Benny Benjamin, Richard Allen and Uriel Jones, the guitarists Robert White, Eddie Willis and Joe Messina and percussionist Jack Ashford. Most were black musicians from Detroit, but white musicians played with them too. According to Hunter the name came from Benjamin, who shouted from the stairs of the studio after a session: you're all the Funk Brothers.

In the small basement studio, the Snake Pit, they played on hits such as Heat Wave, Baby Love, My Girl, I Heard It Through the Grapevine, Ain't No Mountain High Enough and Papa Was a Rollin' Stone. Their sound formed the basis of the Motown sound: Jamerson's bouncy, melodic bass lines, a solid backbeat with tambourine, and guitars that played short and tight. They often played with jazz experience, which made the songs supple and lively. Even so, their names did not appear on the sleeves. Only on What's Going On by Marvin Gaye in 1971 were the musicians credited.

In 1972 Berry Gordy moved the label to Los Angeles. Some of the musicians only heard about it through a note on the studio door. Only with the documentary Standing in the Shadows of Motown from 2002 did they receive recognition. Jamerson and Benjamin were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and the group received a Grammy for their entire body of work.
artiest/the-funk-brothers.listen: Listen to My Girl by The Temptations. Pay particular attention to the bass of James Jamerson and the drums beneath the vocals: together they form the heart of the Motown sound.

artiest/the-hacker.text:
The Hacker is the stage name of Michel Amato, a French electroclash and techno producer from Grenoble. He began making music in 1989, at the age of seventeen. At first he was influenced by Duran Duran, and later he discovered the dark side of electronic music through Cabaret Voltaire and D.A.F. His name comes from a track by Jeff Mills. He was also influenced by Kraftwerk, The Cure, Depeche Mode and the French rave scene of the early 1990s. In 1998 he founded his own label Goodlife Records with friends.

His breakthrough came through a collaboration with Caroline Hervé, known as Miss Kittin. DJ Hell signed them in 1997 to his label International DJ Gigolo. The EPs Champagne (1998) and Intimités (1999) were an immediate success in Germany. Champagne contained 1982 and Frank Sinatra, which quickly became anthems of electroclash. The album First Album (2001) made them known worldwide. The Hacker also made remixes for among others Marc Almond, Fischerspooner and Air. His own albums are Mélodies en Sous-Sol (2000), Electronic Existentialist (2000) and Rêves mécaniques (2004).

After a break Miss Kittin and The Hacker got back together in 2007, with the double A-side Hometown and Dimanche. In 2009 the second duo album, Two, was released. His music links the cool machines of electro with the pop songs of new wave. In this way he belongs among the producers who, in the years around 2000, brought electronic music back to the clubs and to pop music.
artiest/the-hacker.listen: Listen to Frank Sinatra by Miss Kittin & The Hacker and notice how the electronic beat and the vocals together carry the song. Can you hear why this became a club track?

artiest/the-hanoi-ca-tru-thai-ha-ensembl.text:
The Hanoi Ca Trù Thai Ha Ensemble plays ca trù, a traditional Vietnamese chamber music from the north of the country. Little is known with certainty about the ensemble itself, and the available source dealt with Vietnamese music in general. This text is therefore mainly about the music the group plays. It comes from a long tradition of artistic songs performed by female singers, with a small accompanying group.

In ca trù the voice is central. The singer beats the rhythm with a small bamboo percussion instrument, the phách. A long, three-stringed lute, the đàn đáy, accompanies her with loose, sharp tones. A connoisseur of the music plays a small drum and comments on the singing with short strikes. The lyrics are poems, such as the hát nói, a verse form with a free structure. The voice often moves in long, ornamented lines with subtle vibrato. The whole sounds restrained and sober, and it is all about the refinement of every small detail.

Ca trù was long threatened with disappearance and is now actively protected. In School of Rock the ensemble represents the literary chamber music of Vietnam, far from the country's popular music.
artiest/the-hanoi-ca-tru-thai-ha-ensembl.listen: Listen to Muou, Hát Nói. Notice the voice moving slowly and ornamentally through the poem, and the short, sharp tones of the lute and the percussion instrument.

artiest/the-harry-j-all-stars.text:
The Harry J. All Stars were the session band of the Jamaican reggae producer Harry J. His real name was Harry Zephaniah Johnson; he was born in Westmoreland Parish in 1945 and first played bass in the group The Virtues. He then worked as an insurance salesman, until in 1968 he produced No More Heartaches by The Beltones, one of the first reggae songs ever recorded. Thanks to an arrangement with Coxsone Dodd he was allowed to use the Studio One studio.

In October 1969 he had success in England with The Liquidator, recorded with his session band, the Harry J All Stars. The instrumental reached number nine on the British chart and returned to it in 1980. It became one of the anthems of the emerging skinhead culture, along with other instrumental hits released through his own series on Trojan Records. In the early 1970s another big success followed with the vocal duo Bob and Marcia and the song Young, Gifted and Black.

In 1972 Johnson sold his record shop and started his own recording studio on Roosevelt Avenue in Kingston. Bob Marley & the Wailers recorded several albums there between 1973 and 1976, including Catch a Fire and Rastaman Vibration. Burning Spear, the Heptones, Augustus Pablo and Johnny Nash also worked there. The name Harry J thus stands for two things: an instrumental reggae hit that won over audiences in England, and a studio where the sound of 1970s reggae was captured. Johnson died in 2013.
artiest/the-harry-j-all-stars.listen: Listen to The Liquidator and notice how an instrumental without vocals still has a clear theme. What do you remember after hearing it once?

artiest/the-heliocentrics.text:
The Heliocentrics are an English music collective from London that combines funk, jazz, psychedelia and influences from library music. The group centres on drummer and producer Malcolm Catto, bassist Jake Ferguson, guitarist Adrian Owusu and multi-instrumentalist Jack Yglesias. Library music is music originally made for use in film and television, and that sense of cinematic atmosphere comes through in their work.

The debut album Out There was released in 2007 on Now-Again Records. They then collaborated with the Ethiopian musician Mulatu Astatke on the album Inspiration Information (2009). That album received the Gilles Peterson Worldwide album of the year award that year. The pianist Jamie Cullum included it in 2013 in his list of five essential jazz albums. There was also the soundtrack Lloyd Miller & The Heliocentrics (2010) and a collaboration with Orlando Julius. The group played on a track on The Outsider by DJ Shadow, from 2006.

In 2013 13 Degrees of Reality was released on Stones Throw. In 2017 came A World of Masks, with vocals by Barbora Patkova, and the film music for the British documentary The Sunshine Makers. In 2020 Infinity of Now and Telemetric Sounds followed, and in 2023 Legna, a collaboration with The Gaslamp Killer. The Heliocentrics show how jazz, African music and funk can together form a sound of their own.
artiest/the-heliocentrics.listen: Listen to a track from Inspiration Information and notice how the band combines the Ethiopian music of Mulatu Astatke with funk and jazz. Which instruments do you hear first?

artiest/the-hep-stars.text:
The Hep Stars were a Swedish rock band, formed in Stockholm in 1963. In 1965 and 1966 they were the most successful Swedish pop group singing in English. Outside Scandinavia the band is known above all as the starting point of keyboardist and composer Benny Andersson, later known from ABBA. The founders were drummer Christer Pettersson and bassist Lennart Hegland. The group was first called Quartet Yep. The name Hep Stars comes from a line in Razzle Dazzle by Bill Haley.

The classic line-up consisted of singer Svenne Hedlund, guitarist and singer Janne Frisk, Andersson on keyboards, Hegland on bass and Pettersson on drums. In 1965 Cadillac, Farmer John and A Tribute To Buddy Holly were in the top four of the radio chart at the same time. Hedlund became Sweden's first real pop star. The group played covers at first, but later also recorded songs by Andersson, such as No Response, which reached number three. In 1967 came the success of I Natt Jag Drömde, a Swedish version of Last Night I Had a Strangest Dream, a song that divided rock fans.

Because of business problems and a changing market the group began to aim at a broader audience. Frisk left in early 1969 and Björn Ulvaeus of the Hootenanny Singers took his place. In August 1969 the band gave its last concert. Andersson and Ulvaeus then continued to write together, first as a team for Polar Music and as the duo Björn & Benny. That eventually led to ABBA.
artiest/the-hep-stars.listen: Listen to Cadillac and notice the band's driving rock-and-roll energy and the voice of Svenne Hedlund. What tells you that this is a group from the 1960s?

artiest/the-hives.text:
The Hives are a Swedish garage rock band, formed in Fagersta in 1993 by the brothers Per and Niklas Almqvist. Per performs as Howlin' Pelle Almqvist, Niklas as Nicholaus Arson. The other members are Vigilante Carlstroem, Dr. Matt Destruction and Chris Dangerous. Their name came from drummer Chris, who read the word for the skin condition in a dictionary. In 1995 they signed with the Swedish label Burning Heart Records, and in 1997 the debut album Barely Legal was released.

Their breakthrough came with Veni Vidi Vicious (2000) and the single Hate to Say I Told You So, which is regarded as their signature song. The members described the album as a velvet glove with brass knuckles. After the compilation Your New Favourite Band from 2001, which reached number seven in England, they became known worldwide during the garage rock revival. In 2004 came Tyrannosaurus Hives, with among others Walk Idiot Walk. Then came The Black and White Album (2007), Lex Hives (2012), The Death of Randy Fitzsimmons (2023) and The Hives Forever Forever The Hives (2025).

The Hives always wear matching black-and-white suits and are known for their energetic, idiosyncratic concerts. Critics have called them one of the best live acts in rock of the past twenty years. The line-up remained the same from 1993 to 2013. Their music shows that guitar rock with a simple idea and a lot of energy can still convince.
artiest/the-hives.listen: Listen to Hate to Say I Told You So and notice the fierce energy of the vocals and the guitars. Can you hear what the members meant by the description velvet glove with brass knuckles?

artiest/the-hootenanny-singers.text:
The Hootenanny Singers were a popular Swedish folk group from Västervik, formed in 1961. Members included Björn Ulvaeus, who later played in ABBA, Johan Karlberg, Tonny Rooth and Hansi Schwarz. For an LP released in the United States in 1966 the group was called The Northern Lights. In 1964 they first appeared on the Swedish TV programme Hylands Hörna, with a song set to a text by the poet Dan Andersson, Jag väntar vid min mila.

An early hit was Gabrielle, based on the Russian song May There Always Be Sunshine by Arkady Ostrovsky. Because there were no international copyright agreements at the time, songs from the Soviet Union were regarded as free to use. Stig Anderson and Bengt Bernhag of the production company Polar Music claimed the arrangement and lyric credits, which Russian media later called plagiarism. The song reached number five in Sweden and was also recorded in German, Finnish, Italian, Dutch and English.

Through many appearances on open-air stages in Sweden the group became popular. They had many hits on the Svensktoppen chart. Omkring tiggarn från Luossa stayed on that chart for fifty-two weeks, from November 1972 to November 1973, a record. Johan Karlberg stopped at the end of the 1960s to take over his father's business. The album På tre man hand from 1969 contains songs that Ulvaeus also released as a solo single. The group shows where one of the later ABBA members gained his first experience of songs and the stage.
artiest/the-hootenanny-singers.listen: Listen to Gabrielle and notice the simple, folk-like melody. The song is based on a Russian song: why might such a melody work in several languages?

artiest/the-human-league.text:
The Human League are an English synth-pop band from Sheffield, formed in 1977. Ian Craig Marsh and Martyn Ware, two computer operators who knew each other from a youth project, bought a synthesizer together and combined pop music such as glam rock and Motown with avant-garde electronics. They brought in their old school friend Philip Oakey as singer, even though he had never sung before. He worked as a hospital porter and stood out for his clothes. The name comes from the board game StarForce: Alpha Centauri. Adrian Wright joined the group as projectionist and visual director.

In 1979 the group signed with Virgin Records. Reproduction was released in 1979 and Travelogue in 1980. Marsh and Ware then left to start Heaven 17. Oakey and Wright rebuilt the group, with female singers Joanne Catherall and Susan Ann Sulley, bassist Ian Burden and guitarist Jo Callis. This produced Dare in 1981, with The Sound of the Crowd, Love Action (I Believe in Love), Open Your Heart and Don't You Want Me. The last was a number one in the United Kingdom and in the United States. In 1982 they received a Brit Award for best British breakthrough act. Later came Mirror Man, Fascination and The Lebanon, and in 1986 Human, again an American number one. Tell Me When from 1995 was a later hit.

Philip Oakey has been the only constant member since 1977. Today the group is in effect a trio of Oakey, Catherall and Sulley. As an early technopop band The Human League received a lot of airplay on MTV, and they are regarded as a leading name of the second British invasion of the United States. Their music showed that synthesizers did not have to be cold machines, but could also carry warm, danceable pop songs.
artiest/the-human-league.listen: Listen to Don't You Want Me by The Human League. Notice how the duet between Oakey and Sulley works like a short story, with almost only electronic sounds beneath it.

artiest/the-hunters.text:
The Hunters were a British instrumental band of the late 1950s and early 1960s. They came from the area around Cheshunt in Hertfordshire and emerged from the remains of The Parker Royal Five. The line-up consisted of drummer Norman Sheffield, rhythm guitarist Norman Stracey, lead guitarist Brian Parker and bassist John Rogers. The group worked as a backing band for American stars touring England, such as Bobby Rydell and Jimmy Jones, and for British artists such as Frank Ifield and The Avons.

Their first big hit was Sweet Dreams, as backing band to singer Dave Sampson, which reached number 29 on the British chart in May 1960. Teen Scene then came out under their own name on Fontana, which did not make the chart. Even so, their singles sold enough for two albums, in 1961 and 1962. In total they released several singles and albums between 1960 and 1964. The band also once played behind Cliff Richard in place of The Shadows, when they were unable to appear because of a car accident. Their sound was therefore often mistaken for that of The Shadows, but this was down to the guitars and equipment of the time, with which more bands sounded that way.

After The Hunters, Parker, Rogers and Stracey played in The Roulettes, Adam Faith's backing band. Parker also founded Unit 4 + 2. Drummer Norman Sheffield started Trident Studios in London with his brother, where Queen later recorded among others, a band he managed in its early years. The Dutch rock band Golden Earring is named after their single Golden Earrings. In 2009 Teen Scene sounded again in the film An Education.
artiest/the-hunters.listen: Listen to Teen Scene and notice the electric guitars without vocals. Can you hear why this song was often mistaken for The Shadows?

artiest/the-i-threes.text:
The I-Threes were the female vocal trio that accompanied Bob Marley after Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer left the Wailers in 1974. The three members were Rita Marley, Bob Marley's wife, Judy Mowatt and Marcia Griffiths. The name is a variant on the Rastafarian concept I and I, which refers to the divine in every person.

Marley continued with a new line-up that also included the brothers Aston and Carlton Barrett, the guitarists Junior Marvin and Al Anderson, keyboard players and a percussionist. The I-Threes provided the backing vocals. Their first album with the band was Natty Dread from 1974, the first without Tosh and Wailer, with among others No Woman, No Cry, Lively Up Yourself and Them Belly Full (But We Hungry). In 1975 a live version of No Woman, No Cry from the Lyceum Theatre in London became the group's first successful single outside reggae circles.

The I-Threes stayed with Marley until his death in 1981, after which his group ceased. Later they also made records under their own name, such as Beginning (1986) and Songs of Bob Marley (1995). In this way they formed a constant part of the sound with which reggae conquered the world in the 1970s.
artiest/the-i-threes.listen: Listen to No Woman, No Cry in the live version by Bob Marley & the Wailers and notice the backing vocals of the I-Threes beneath Marley's voice. What do the women's voices add to the song?

artiest/the-impressions.text:
The Impressions were an American group, formed in 1958, with gospel, R&B, doo-wop and soul in their repertoire. They began as The Roosters, formed by Sam Gooden and the brothers Richard and Arthur Brooks from Chattanooga. In Chicago Jerry Butler and Curtis Mayfield joined, who knew each other from a church choir. At first the group was called Jerry Butler & the Impressions, and their first hit, For Your Precious Love in 1958, reached number 3 on the R&B chart. When Butler left, Mayfield became the group's lead singer and writer.

At ABC-Paramount they had a big hit in 1961 with Gypsy Woman. With producer Johnny Pate a fuller soul sound then emerged, which can be heard on It's All Right (1963). In 1964 came Keep on Pushing, the first of Mayfield's songs about black pride, and in 1965 People Get Ready, their best-known song, with a lot of gospel in it. Their songs became inspiring anthems of the Civil Rights Movement. In 1968 We're a Winner reached number one on the R&B chart.

Mayfield left in 1970 for a solo career, with among other things the music for Super Fly. The group continued with new singers and in 1974 had another number one with Finally Got Myself Together. The Impressions were an example for The Wailers, who took their harmony singing as a model. In 1991 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2018 the group stopped after more than sixty years.
artiest/the-impressions.listen: Listen to People Get Ready and notice the harmony singing and the gospel-like atmosphere. Can you hear how this song sounds like a word of encouragement?
